The imperative φέρε [come], like ἄγε [come], is added to exhortations
The middle form φέρομαι [I carry off for myself] means I take away, I receive.
The passive φέρομαι [I am carried] means I am borne.
I am snatched away.

Similarly Sophocles fr. 669 σιγᾶν ἀνάγκη, κἂν καλὸν φέρῃ στόμα [it is necessary to be silent, even if the mouth bears what is fine] and other examples collected in the Thesaurus vol. 8 p. 716, unless in such places φορεῖν [to carry habitually] should be written with Cobet Mnem. vol. 9 p. 116. "For of all parts of the body φορεῖν [to carry habitually], not φέρειν [to carry], is said, as of the body's dress and ornament φορεῖν [to wear]. We are said φέρειν [to carry] burdens and whatever has weight. Therefore γλῶσσαν φορεῖν [to wear a tongue] is Greek and στόμα φορεῖν [to wear a mouth], as in Alexis in Athenaeus p. 568 c. ἵνα θεωρῶσ᾽ οἱ παρόντες τὸ στόμ᾽ ὡς κομψόν φορεῖ [so that those present may see how elegantly he wears his mouth]."
